fields.title: République Démocratique du Congo: Bulletin d’information - Effets de l’épidémie d’Ebola et de la fermeture de la frontière avec l’Ouganda sur les marchés de Beni et Bunia, Août 2026
fields.body:
**Messages clés**

• L’évolution des prix alimentaires différait entre les deux villes. À Beni, malgré les baisses observées depuis juin, le  
coût médian du panier alimentaire restait en août 37% supérieur à son niveau d’avril. Par contre, à Bunia, aucune  
hausse généralisée des prix alimentaires n’a été observée. La contraction simultanée de la demande, dans un contexte  
de contraintes économiques et de baisse de fréquentation des marchés liée à l’épidémie, pourrait avoir limité la  
transmission des perturbations de l’approvisionnement aux prix.

• Les tensions sur les produits sanitaires étaient plus importantes à Bunia qu’à Beni. Le prix médian déclaré du gel  
hydroalcoolique avait augmenté de 67% à Bunia contre 20% à Beni, tandis que celui des masques chirurgicaux avait  
doublé à Bunia mais était resté stable à Beni.

• Les contraintes de liquidités (accès aux espèces et augmentation des frais de retraits) étaient particulièrement  
marquées à Bunia, tant pour les commerçants que pour leurs clients : 15/27 commerçants ont identifié le manque de  
liquidités comme une difficulté de réapprovisionnement, tandis que 17/27 ont rapporté un recours accru au crédit de la  
part de leurs clients depuis le début de l’épidémie.

fields.title: In Ituri, MONUSCO protects thousands of civilians fleeing armed violence
fields.body:
More than 3,100 civilians have sought refuge in the United Nations Organization Stabilization Mission in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (MONUSCO) temporary base in Rhoo, in Djugu Territory, Ituri, following violent clashes between armed groups.

The violence broke out on the evening of Sunday, September 27, in the localities of Nyampala and Rhoo, involving, among others, elements of the CODECO armed group and the Convention for the Popular Revolution (CRP). The rapidly deteriorating security situation triggered an exodus of civilians, including internally displaced people who were already living at the Rhoo site.

Fearing for their safety, thousands of people, including women, children and elderly people, headed toward MONUSCO’s temporary operating base located near the displacement site. Some spent the night inside the base, while others sought refuge in its immediate vicinity, all benefiting from the protection of the Bangladeshi peacekeepers deployed there.

“*We want to save our lives, which is why we came to MONUSCO for protection,*” said Vyanye Dirokpa, a displaced person from the Rhoo site, in an interview with Radio Okapi.

Another resident highlighted the importance of the peacekeepers’ presence in the area: “*If MONUSCO had not been here, things would have been worse. We might not even be alive today.*”

**Protection and emergency assistance**

According to MONUSCO, approximately 3,100 civilians, including nearly 1,600 women and 900 children, benefited from protection measures implemented by MONUSCO as fighting intensified in the surrounding areas.

The Bangladeshi peacekeepers immediately secured the area, received displaced people, and provided temporary shelter and physical protection to vulnerable families. They also strengthened their presence around the displacement site and in neighboring localities, while maintaining close coordination with local authorities, community leaders, and the FARDC.

The UN mission also provided emergency medical assistance to civilians affected by the violence. Nine people received first aid at the Rhoo base, including two men with gunshot wounds, two young girls, a ten-month-old infant, and four women. MONUSCO medical teams continued to provide care to those requiring treatment, while peacekeepers continued to ensure the safety of displaced people.

**A situation that remains volatile**

On the morning of Monday, September 28, exchanges of gunfire were still being reported in several localities in the area, including as far as Blukwa, located approximately four kilometers from Rhoo. The persistent insecurity prompted more civilians to move closer to MONUSCO positions to seek protection.

According to security sources, suspected CODECO elements reportedly set fire to several homes in central Blukwa. MONUSCO peacekeepers, in coordination with the FARDC, intervened to repel the attackers and limit the damage caused.

**Civilian protection also strengthened in Gina**

Earlier on Monday, September 28, the locality of Gina, located approximately 30 kilometers south of Bunia, also experienced security incidents.

Fighting broke out between the FARDC and elements of the CRP, and many civilians also sought refuge in front of the MONUSCO base.

The Nepalese peacekeepers deployed in Gina immediately strengthened their protection measures. Patrols were conducted along the roads connecting Panga Panga, Risasi, Gina and Nyampala, as well as along National Road 27, in order to protect civilians, prevent further attacks and reassure affected communities.

Thanks to MONUSCO’s reinforced presence, in support of the FARDC, the return of residents to their homes gradually resumed in some localities. Commercial activities, particularly in markets, also began to return to normal by midday.

Following this new escalation of violence in Djugu Territory, local authorities and community actors are calling on armed groups to honor their commitments to ending hostilities and upholding the ceasefire.

***- Joël Bofengo***

fields.title: Nutrition Cluster 2025 - 2026 Malnutrition Overview in the North and South West Regions of Cameroon (18 Sep 2026)
fields.body:
**SUMMARY OF SAM SCREENED IN 2026**

In 2026, the Nutrition Cluster screened 128,940 children (54% girls and 46% boys) for malnutrition. A total of 7,015 (5.44%) children were identified with SAM out of which 1,563 (22.22%) were admitted, that it 866 (12%) girls and 697 (10%) boys of the total SAM cases. A total of 77.78% of the SAM cases identified in 2026 are still unattended.

Out of the 128,940 children screened, 3,937 (3%) were found to be Moderately Acutely Malnourished (MAM), with an admission rate of 12% (470) of the total MAM, comprising 246 (52%) girls and 224 (48%) boys. This falls short of expectations, with 97% unadmitted.

**SUMMARY OF SAM SCREENED IN 2025**

In 2025, the Nutrition Cluster screened 342,057 children (53% girls and 47% boys) for malnutrition. A total of 3739 (1.09%) children were identified with SAM out of which 3,670 (98.15%) were admitted, that it 2,102 (56%) girls and 1,568 (42%) boys of the total SAM cases. This presents an excellent admission rate compared to 2026 plagued by funding scarcity.

Out of the 342,057 children screened, 28,973 (8.47%) were found to be Moderately Acutely Malnourished (MAM), with an admission rate of 59% (17,056) of the total MAM, comprising 9,800 (57%) girls and 7,256 (43%) boys. This presents a good admission rate compared to 2026, during which only 3% of MAM cases were admitted.

**These findings call for a dire need for timely nutrition interventions to continue to save the lives of children 6 to 59 months old in the NWSW Regions. THE TIME TO ACT IS NOW**

fields.title: Democratic Republic of the Congo: Current and anticipated indirect humanitarian impacts of the Ebola outbreak (ACAPS Thematic Report 28 September 2026)
fields.body:
CRISIS OVERVIEW

Since its declaration in May 2026, the outbreak of Ebola – caused by Bundibugyo virus – in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) has spread to seven provinces: Bas-Uele, Haut-Uele, Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, Sud-Ubangi, and Tshopo (INSP 26/09/2026; WHO 14/08/2026). By 25 September, the Government had recorded 7,989 confirmed cases and 3,852 deaths, corresponding to a reported crude case fatality ratio of 48.2%. This is the largest and fastest-growing Ebola outbreak ever recorded in the DRC, with transmission continuing to outpace control efforts (INSP 26/09/2026; WHO 24/08/2026). Beyond its direct toll, the outbreak is already reducing the use of essential health services in the worst-affected areas. Between April–June 2026, use of routinely monitored primary healthcare services fell by 42% across Ituri’s four main hotspots of Bunia, Mongbwalu, Nizi, and Rwampara, and by around 13% across the province as a whole, with no comparable seasonal decline recorded a year earlier (UNICEF 06/08/2026). Nutrition services followed the same trend, with preschool consultations declining by 20.4% and the number of severe acute malnutrition cases treated declining by 17.8% in June 2026 compared with June 2025. The latter decline may reflect reduced access to nutrition services and screening rather than an improvement in children’s nutritional status (Nutrition Cluster 03/09/2026). Service availability has also declined locally. In the Héritage health area of Limani, Djugu territory, nine of 12 health posts have suspended activities after becoming overwhelmed by the daily influx of patients, reducing surrounding communities’ access to basic healthcare (Radio Okapi 15/07/2026). The indirect impact of the outbreak reflects both reduced health service availability – as a result of staffing and operational pressures – and reduced demand, as fear of infection and isolation discourages care-seeking. Current reporting identifies fear of infection, movement restrictions, stigma, the temporary reorganisation of health services, and the mobilisation of personnel for the response as factors affecting the use and continuity of routine health and nutrition services (UNICEF 06/08/2026; Nutrition Cluster 03/09/2026). The outbreak and its response also place additional demand on health workers, facilities, laboratories, referral systems, transport, protective equipment, and supplies needed to maintain routine care. Available evidence does not establish that these resources have been systematically withdrawn from non-Ebola programmes, but shortages and competing demands may disrupt consultations, referrals, and the continuity of care (WHO 20/08/2026; Mulenga-Cilundika et al. 12/10/2022). These pressures are affecting a health system in which facility closures, shortages of medical products, insecurity, and funding cuts had already left large numbers of people without access to healthcare and nutrition services (OCHA 28/01/2026).

source.name: ACAPS
source.spanish_name: ACAPS

fields.title: Eastern Chad: Sudan Situation – Flash Updates #57
fields.body:
**Context**  
  
The security situation along Chad’s borders remains a concern, while conditions inside the country remain generally stable. The eastern provinces of Sila, Ouaddaï, Wadi Fira and Ennedi Est continue to be affected by the spillover of the conflict in neighbouring Sudan. In addition to the continued arrival of refugees fleeing violence in Sudan, several security incidents linked to the conflict have been reported in Chad since late August, including drone strikes in Wadi Fira and Ennedi Est. On 11 September, a Chadian national was reportedly killed near Kulbus in Wadi Fira by members of the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), and reports of kidnappings have also emerged from the border area.  
  
At the same time, worsening climatic conditions and the impact of drought, described by the World Food Programme (WFP) as one of the most severe in the region since 1984, continue to undermine livelihoods, reduce agricultural production and drive additional population movements towards eastern Chad. In response, the Chadian Government recently conducted an assessment mission in the eastern provinces to evaluate the extent of the rainfall deficit and identify appropriate mitigation measures. Proposed actions include the exemption of customs duties on selected essential food commodities and the targeted distribution of cereals to the most affected households.  
  
The drought situation was also discussed during meetings between provincial authorities in Ouaddaï and the UNHCR Regional Director for East and Horn of Africa and the Great Lakes, who also serves as Regional Coordinator for the Sudan Refugee Situation, during his mission to Chad from 17 to 21 September 2026. Chadian authorities expressed concern over the humanitarian and socio-economic consequences of the climate crisis, which are compounding pressures arising from the continued influx of Sudanese refugees.  
  
Within the country, incidents of criminality and petty crime, including armed robberies, assaults and explosions caused by explosive devices, continue to be reported in some refugee-hosting areas. Meanwhile, heavy seasonal rains and rising wadi water levels are restricting access to several locations in eastern Chad, creating additional challenges for humanitarian operations.  
  
Two Safe and Secure Approaches in Field Environments (SSAFE) training sessions were conducted for 61 participants, and two additional sessions, organized in collaboration with WFP, are planned for October.

fields.title: RD Congo : Ituri : le Coordonnateur humanitaire appelle à préserver la sécurité et la dignité des personnes déplacées de Kigonze
fields.body: **Kinshasa, le 27 septembre 2026 –** Le Coordonnateur humanitaire en République démocratique du Congo, M. Damien Mama, exprime sa vive préoccupation face à la détérioration de la situation sur le site de Kigonze, à Bunia (province de l’Ituri), qui accueille près de 19 000 personnes déplacées. Depuis le 20 septembre, des incidents de sécurité et de protection y ont été signalés, poussant de nombreuses familles à quitter le site. « Des familles qui ont déjà tout perdu doivent pouvoir trouver sécurité et dignité là où elles sont venues chercher refuge. Les sites de personnes déplacées doivent préserver leur caractère civil et humanitaire, et toute solution concernant l’avenir de ces familles doit être volontaire, sûre et digne », a déclaré M. Mama. Le Coordonnateur humanitaire est en contact étroit avec les autorités nationales et provinciales, dont il salue la disponibilité, et poursuit avec elles un dialogue constructif afin de garantir la protection des personnes déplacées et de faciliter la réponse humanitaire. L’insécurité a également entravé l’accès humanitaire au site, limitant la capacité des organisations à évaluer les besoins, à fournir une assistance vitale et à assurer des services essentiels de protection. Kigonze figure également parmi les sites couverts par la riposte contre l’épidémie d’Ebola en cours. La dispersion des familles et les restrictions d’accès risquent de compliquer la surveillance épidémiologique et les efforts de contrôle de l’épidémie. En Ituri, plus de 1,1 million de personnes sont déplacées par les conflits et les violences, dont plus de 373 000 vivent sur des sites de déplacés. Le Coordonnateur humanitaire réitère son appel à la protection des civils et à un accès humanitaire sûr et sans entrave, et réaffirme l’engagement de la communauté humanitaire à soutenir les efforts des autorités en faveur des personnes déplacées.

fields.title: Disease Outbreak News: Ebola disease caused by Bundibugyo virus, Democratic Republic of the Congo (25 September 2026)
fields.body:
**Situation at a glance**

Since the last Disease Outbreak News was published on 11 September 2026, the Bundibugyo virus outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has expanded further, with two additional health zones affected. These include Bulu health zone in a new province, Sud Ubangi, located on the north-west part of the country and Dungu health zone in Haut-Uélé province, bordering South Sudan. This brings the total number of affected health zones to 63 across seven provinces out of 26 provinces of the country: Bas-Uélé, Haut-Uélé, Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, Sud Ubangi and Tshopo. This latest geographic expansion increases the risk of cross-border transmission. As of 23 September 2026, the Democratic Republic of the Congo has reported 7890 confirmed cases, including 3799 deaths, resulting in a crude case fatality ratio (CFR) of 48.1%. At the national level, the number of new cases reported each day remains high. However, the situation varies across the country, with some provinces and health zones experiencing much higher levels of transmission than others. The continuously high CFR, and especially the continuous high rate of deaths occurring in communities, highlights the seriousness of the disease and the persistent challenges in timely case detection and access to early and adequate patient care. These delays can contribute to preventable illness and deaths among people in affected and newly affected areas, while also allowing transmission to continue within households, communities, and healthcare settings.

**Description of the situation**

Since the previous [Disease Outbreak News](https://www.who.int/emergencies/disease-outbreak-news/item/2026-DON617) was published on 11 September 2026, an additional 1133 confirmed cases, including 532 confirmed deaths, have been reported in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. The seven-day moving average shows a resurgence in early September followed by a decline over the most recent reporting days. However, the aggregate national trend conceals substantial variation in transmission intensity across affected provinces and health zones.

As of 23 September, the Democratic Republic of the Congo has reported a total of 7890 confirmed cases, including 3799 deaths (CFR 48.1%). A total of 1966 patients have recovered to date.

Confirmed cases have been reported from 63 health zones across seven provinces, with 48 health zones from six provinces reporting at least one case in the last 21 days. Ituri remains the most affected province, with 28 of its 36 health zones reporting cases, followed by North Kivu (16/34), Tshopo (7/23), Haut-Uélé (7/13), Bas-Uélé (3/11), South Kivu (1/34), and Sud Ubangi (1/16). No new cases have been reported from South Kivu province since 29 May 2026. Dungu Health Zone in Haut-Uélé province and Bulu in Sud Ubangi are the most recently affected areas. As of 23 September, 70 new confirmed cases had been reported in the preceding 24 hours from 26 health zones located in Ituri, North Kivu, Haut-Uélé, Bas Uélé and Tshopo provinces.

Ituri continues to be the epicentre of the outbreak, accounting for 6032 confirmed cases since the start of the outbreak, including 868 new confirmed cases reported in the previous 21 days, as of 23 September. North Kivu is the second most affected province, with a cumulative number of 1480 confirmed cases, including 567 reported in the last 21 days, as of 23 September. North Kivu province continues to report the highest CFR (59.7%) observed in this outbreak; and investigations are ongoing to better understand the factors contributing to this elevated mortality rate.

In Ituri, case incidence continues to decline gradually from the peak observed in mid-August, although transmission remains at elevated levels. North Kivu, in contrast, has experienced a substantial increase in incidence, reaching its highest reported level in mid-September, followed by a decline in recent reporting days. Haut-Uélé continues to demonstrate sustained transmission, albeit at levels below the peak recorded in late August, while Tshopo is showing renewed transmission activity following a period of low incidence. In Bas-Uélé, transmission remains sporadic, whereas no recent evidence of transmission has been reported in Sud-Kivu. Sud Ubangi is the seventh province to report a confirmed case of BVD, with one case that was reported on 10 September (Figure 2).

The number of individuals requiring follow-up as contact has also risen considerably with the expansion of the outbreak. As of 23 September, 83.4% of identified contacts were successfully monitored during the previous 24 hours with 26 980 contacts seen out of 32 342 requiring follow up. The large volume of contacts under surveillance highlights the extent of potential exposure within affected communities and the substantial demands placed on response operations.

The response is being implemented in a challenging humanitarian environment, where conflict, insecurity, displacement, and limited access to basic services continue to affect outbreak control. These constraints continue to hamper surveillance, case finding, contact tracing, infection prevention and control, and timely access to appropriate care, thereby limiting the overall effectiveness of response activities.

**Epidemiology**

Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD) is a severe Ebola disease caused by the Bundibugyo virus, one of the *Orthoebolavirus* species. It is a zoonotic disease, with fruit bats suspected to be the natural reservoir.

Human infection is thought to occur through close contact with the blood or secretions of infected wildlife, such as bats or non-human primates, and it subsequently spreads from person-to-person through direct contact with the blood, secretions, organs, or other bodily fluids of infected individuals or contaminated surfaces and materials. Transmission is particularly amplified in health-care settings when IPC measures are inadequate and during unsafe burial practices involving direct contact with deceased individuals.

The incubation period for BVD ranges from two to 21 days, and infected individuals are not infectious until symptom onset. Early symptoms such as fever, fatigue, muscle pain, headache, and sore throat are non-specific, which complicates clinical diagnosis and can delay detection. These symptoms then progress to gastrointestinal symptoms, organ dysfunction, and, in some cases, haemorrhagic manifestations.

The historical CFR from the past two BVD outbreaks, reported in Uganda and in the Democratic Republic of the Congo in 2007 and 2012, were 30% and 50%, respectively.

Differentiating BVD from other endemic febrile illnesses such as malaria is challenging without laboratory confirmation using polymerase chain reaction (PCR) or antigen- or antibody-based assays. Outbreak control relies on rapid case identification, isolation and care, contact tracing, safe burials and strong community engagement, as no approved vaccines or specific treatments currently exist for BVD.

Since first detected in May 2026, this BVD outbreak has rapidly evolved into a large and geographically expanding epidemic in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, with sustained transmission, high mortality and an increasing risk of further international spread. The current outbreak is the second documented Bundibugyo virus disease outbreak in the country, after the 2012 outbreak, and the largest Ebola disease outbreak ever recorded in the Democratic Republic of the Congo irrespective of Ebola virus species. The population at greatest risk of exposure is concentrated in communities living in and moving through the health areas with active transmission.

**Public health response**

For detailed information about the ongoing public health response actions by the Ministry of Health, WHO and partners please refer to the latest situation reports published by the WHO Regional Office for Africa: [Ongoing outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo | WHO | Regional Office for Africa](https://www.afro.who.int/health-topics/ebola-disease/outbreak-drc-26)

Health authorities in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, in collaboration with WHO and partners, are continuing to implement and coordinate extensive public health measures, including disease surveillance, laboratory testing, infection prevention and control, clinical care, community engagement, research, logistics and support for response interventions and essential health services, engaging donors and mobilizing additional resources to address critical funding gaps and sustain response operations across affected and at-risk areas. A substantial scale-up is ongoing across all response pillars to get ahead of the outbreak.

**WHO risk assessment**

On 14 August 2026, WHO reassessed the risk of the outbreak of BVD, incorporating newly available information on the evolving situation. The risk for countries sharing land borders with the Democratic Republic of the Congo was separated from the risk for other countries in the African Region.

The risk in the Democratic Republic of the Congo was assessed as very high, the risk for countries sharing land borders with the Democratic Republic of the Congo was assessed as high, and the risks for the rest of the African region and at the global level was again assessed as low.

**WHO advice**

Based on the currently available information, WHO advises against any restriction of travel to, or trade with, affected countries. WHO continues to closely monitor and, where necessary, verify travel and trade measures in relation to this event.

The updated [Temporary Recommendations](https://www.who.int/news/item/24-08-2026-second-meeting-of-the-ihr-emergency-committee-on-the-epidemic-of-ebola-bundibugyo-virus-disease-in-the-democratic-republic-of-the-congo-temporary-recommendations) issued to States Parties on 24 August 2026 underscore the importance of coordinated outbreak control, strengthened cross‑border collaboration, and sustained surveillance and preparedness to prevent further regional spread and ensure an effective public health response. Rapid recognition of cases, testing and optimized supportive care can reduce mortality, and improve community perceptions and acceptance of health care within the response.

fields.title: IOM: Multi-Country Bundibugyo Ebola Virus Disease Outbreak - Situation Report No. 19 (14 - 20 September 2026)
fields.body:
**SITUATION OVERVIEW**

According to the Ministry of Health of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), as of 20 September 2026, the Bundibugyo Ebola virus disease (BVD) outbreak had resulted in 7,733 confirmed cases, 3,732 deaths and 1,902 recoveries, representing a case fatality rate of 48.3 per cent. Since the beginning of the outbreak, 63 of 167 health zones (37.7%) across seven provinces have reported at least one confirmed case, while 55 health zones across five provinces remain classified as active transmission zones.

Although several health zones have reported extended periods without detecting new cases, transmission remains concentrated in eastern DRC. A total of 61 newly confirmed cases were reported in Ituri (34), North Kivu (23) and Haut-Uélé (4), with Ituri and North Kivu accounting for 93.4 per cent of all newly reported cases. The continued concentration of transmission in these areas underscores the need to sustain disease surveillance, response and preparedness capacities within affected provinces, while maintaining readiness in neighbouring countries connected through cross-border mobility corridors.

While localized progress has been observed in parts of the response, mortality remains a significant concern. Community deaths continue to account for the majority of newly reported deaths, highlighting ongoing challenges related to early detection, timely referral and access to care. These challenges are particularly relevant in settings affected by displacement, insecurity and population movement, where delays in seeking or accessing care may contribute to continued transmission.

fields.title: République centrafricaine : Rapport de situation N° 86, au 22 septembre 2026
fields.body:
**FAITS SAILLANTS**

- Une personne tuée et plusieurs dizaines de personnes enlevées par des hommes armés dans le Haut-Mbomou.
- Environ 2 000 ménages reçoivent une assistance monétaire dans le Mbomou et le Haut-Mbomou.

**CONTEXTE GÉNÉRAL**

Préfecture du Haut-Mbomou – Sud-Est

- Le 17 septembre, des hommes armés ont empêché des organisations humanitaires qui quittaient Zémio d’atteindre Djéma, où elles prévoyaient de reprendre des activités suspendues de longue date en raison de l’insécurité. Les hommes armés ont exigé de l’argent en échange de la liberté de mouvement et ont menacé les membres de la mission humanitaire. Malgré leur volonté de poursuivre la mission, les organisations humanitaires ont dû rebrousser chemin à Kitessa en raison des contraintes sécuritaires. Le 21 septembre, alors que l’équipe retournait à Zémio sur l’axe Mboki-Zémio, des hommes armés ont de nouveau braqué les mêmes travailleurs humanitaires. En conséquence, plus de 20 000 personnes vulnérables vivant à Djéma et le long des axes Zémio-Djéma, Zémio-Dembia et Zémio-Mboki continuent de subir les effets des perturbations de l’assistance humanitaire liées à l’insécurité. Ces incidents surviennent après plus de deux mois de suspension des activités humanitaires depuis juillet 2026, sur fond de dégradation persistante de la situation sécuritaire dans le Haut-Mbomou. Les risques de protection des civils restent élevés, des meurtres, des violences basées sur le genre et des enlèvements continuant d’être signalés. Le Haut-Mbomou demeure la deuxième préfecture la plus touchée par les incidents affectant les acteurs humanitaires.

**BESOINS ET RÉPONSE HUMANITAIRE**

**Eau, hygiène et assainissement (EHA)**

Préfecture de la Bamingui-Bangoran – Nord-Est

- Du 15 au 17 septembre, Plan International a distribué des kits d’hygiène et de dignité ainsi que des caprins à Ndélé-centre, Aliou-Lemena et Bangbali. Six filles âgées de 12 à 17 ans ont reçu des kits comprenant des pagnes, des seaux, des ustensiles de cuisine et des articles de toilette. Par ailleurs, 61 ménages ont reçu chacun deux caprins, soit 122 animaux au total, afin de renforcer leurs moyens de subsistance. Un suivi des activités de relance économique et des moyens de subsistance a également été assuré.

fields.title: Cluster Protection RDC : Points saillants de la situation de protection en République démocratique du Congo du mois d’août 2026
fields.body:
En août 2026, la situation de protection en RDC est demeurée préoccupante, particulièrement dans les provinces de l’Est, où l’insécurité persistante a continué d’exposer les populations civiles à de multiples violations de droits, notamment les atteintes à l’intégrité physique, les enlèvements, les violences sexuelles, les pillages, les extorsions et les restrictions de mouvement liées à la présence de groupes armés.

Les affrontements et opérations militaires au Nord-Kivu, Sud-Kivu, Ituri et Tanganyika ont entraîné de nouveaux déplacements de population et accru les besoins de protection.

Par ailleurs, des tensions communautaires et foncières observées au Maï-Ndombe et au Kwilu rappellent que les risques de protection s’étendent au-delà des zones de conflit armé.

Les femmes, les enfants, les personnes déplacées et retournées demeurent particulièrement vulnérables, tandis que les contraintes sécuritaires continuent de limiter l’accès humanitaire dans certaines localités.

Enfin, la progression de l’épidémie de maladie à virus Ebola a aggravé les vulnérabilités préexistantes des populations déjà affectées par les conflits et les déplacements.

fields.title: Central African Republic: Situation Report No. 86, as of 22 September 2026
fields.body:
**HIGHLIGHTS**

- One person killed and dozens abducted by armed men in Haut-Mbomou.
- Approximately 2,000 households receive cash assistance in Mbomou and Haut-Mbomou.

**GENERAL CONTEXT**

Haut-Mbomou Prefecture - South-East

- On 17 September, armed men prevented humanitarian organizations travelling from Zémio to Djéma, where they had planned to resume activities suspended for an extended period due to insecurity. The armed men demanded money in exchange for freedom of movement and threatened members of the humanitarian mission. Despite efforts to continue the mission, humanitarian actors were forced to turn back at Kitessa because of security constraints. On 21 September, the same humanitarian workers were again ambushed by armed men while returning to Zémio along the Mboki-Zémio road. As a result, more than 20,000 vulnerable people in Djéma and along the Zémio-Djéma, Zémio-Dembia and Zémio-Mboki corridors continue to face disruptions in humanitarian assistance. These incidents occurred after more than two months of humanitarian activity suspensions since July 2026 amid a continued deterioration of the security situation in Haut-Mbomou. Protection risks remain high, with killings, gender-based violence and abductions continuing to be reported. Haut-Mbomou remains the second most affected prefecture by incidents impacting humanitarian actors.

**HUMANITARIAN NEEDS AND RESPONSE**

**WASH**

Bamingui-Bangoran Prefecture - North-East

- From 15 to 17 September, Plan International distributed hygiene and dignity kits, as well as goats, in Ndélé town, Aliou-Lemena and Bangbali. Six girls aged 12 to 17 received kits containing wraps, buckets, cooking utensils and personal hygiene items. In addition, 61 households each received two goats, for a total of 122 animals, to strengthen their livelihoods. Monitoring of livelihood recovery and economic empowerment activities was also conducted.

fields.title: UNICEF Democratic Republic of the Congo Humanitarian Situation Report No. 3 – Ebola Outbreak (Bundibugyo Virus), 31 August
fields.body:
**Highlights**

- UNICEF is scaling up its response from 49 to 60 affected and high-risk health zones, supporting Government-led efforts across community-based surveillance, RCCE, IPC/WASH, nutrition, MHPSS, clinical care, PSEA and continuity of essential services.
- In August, 11,723 community actors, including 6,546 community mobilizers (RECOs), were trained and mobilized on RCCE and community-based surveillance. Since the beginning of the response, a total of 24,750 frontline workers, including 12,555 community mobilizers (RECOs), have been mobilized.
- UNICEF-supported community surveillance networks generated 29,689 alerts in August, representing an 186 per cent increase from the previous reporting period. Contact tracing coverage reached 88 per cent, with 22,499 of 25,560 contacts followed, strengthening outbreak detection and monitoring efforts.
- UNICEF and partners continued to deliver lifesaving support despite operational constraints due to the Ebola outbreak. In August, 126,078 people were reached with essential supplies and emergency health and nutrition assistance through the rapid response mechanism.
- Ahead of the new school year, UNICEF and the Ministry of Education agreed on measures to ensure the safe reopening of schools in Ebola-affected provinces. UNICEF provided technical support to establish reopening standards based on risk assessments of the BVD spread in schools and will support 900 schools with WASH and IPC supplies, MHPSS services, and community awareness activities on Ebola prevention.
- UNICEF requires US$113.5 million for its revised six-month response plan. As of 31 August 2026, US$34.4 million had been mobilized, leaving a US$79 million funding gap, equivalent to 70 per cent of the requirement.

**EPIDEMIOLOGICAL SITUATION UPDATE**

Between 1 and 31 August 2026, the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) reported 2,581 confirmed Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD) cases and 1,420 deaths. As of 31 August, cumulative confirmed cases had reached 6,186, including 3,007 deaths, corresponding to a case fatality ratio (CFR) of 48.6%. The outbreak continued to expand geographically with confirmed cases reported for the first time in Bas-Uélé Province, bringing the number of affected provinces to six (Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, Haut-Uélé,  
Tshopo and Bas-Uélé). During August, an additional 12 health zones reported confirmed cases, increasing the total to 60 affected health zones, representing 39.7 per cent of the country's 151 health zones.

The outbreak is now the largest Ebola outbreak ever recorded in the DRC and the second largest globally. Ituri Province remains the epicentre, accounting for 81.9 per cent of all confirmed cases (5,065) and 2,305 deaths followed by North Kivu (868 cases, 589 deaths) and Haut-Uélé (227 cases, 100 deaths). Transmission also continued in Tshopo, South Kivu and Bas-Uélé. Women and girls represent 53 per cent of reported cases. Children under 17 account for approximately 30.2 per cent of cases and 21.8 per cent of reported deaths, with children under five bearing the greatest burden, representing nearly two-thirds of deaths among children under 18. During August, 42 health workers were affected, underscoring ongoing risks to frontline responders.

L'évaluation multisectorielle des besoins (Multi-Sectoral Needs Assessment, MSNA) 2026 au Cameroun vise à mettre à disposition de la communauté humanitaire des données permettant de comprendre la nature et la sévérité des besoins humanitaires des populations dans les régions de l’Extrême Nord, du Nord-Ouest et du Sud-Ouest au Cameroun, afin d’informer le cycle de programmation humanitaire (HPC 2027).

fields.title: COD: Épidémie - 09-2026 - La République Démocratique du Congo fait face à l'épidémique du choléra orientée à la hausse à l'échelle nationale (2026-09-24)
fields.body:
## **Description**

La République Démocratique du Congo fait face à une dynamique épidémique du choléra orientée à la hausse à l'échelle nationale. Pour la semaine 37, le pays avait enregistré environ 2 200 cas suspects et 14 décès à travers différentes zones de santé. Le bilan cumulé de l'année 2026 dépasse désormais les 41 300 cas suspects et 1 214 décès notifiés sur le territoire national. Au total, 16 des 26 provinces de la RDC ont notifié des foyers épidémiques ou des cas actifs depuis le début de l'année. Durant la semaine 38, l'Institut National de Santé Publique (INSP) identifie 5 provinces prioritaires ayant directement notifié des cas. Le Nord-Kivu constitue l'épicentre majeur de l'épidémie à l'Est, aggravé par l'insécurité et les déplacements massifs de populations. La province du Lualaba enregistre une transmission active au sein du bloc géographique du Grand-Katanga. La province du Tanganyika demeure un foyer sanitaire endémique situé le long du bassin des Grands Lacs. Le Kasaï-Oriental présente une réémergence active de cas nécessitant un suivi particulier dans le Grand-Kasaï. La province de la Mongala confirme l'extension de la maladie le long du corridor fluvial du fleuve Congo. Onze autres provinces (Sud-Kivu, Haut-Katanga, Ituri, Maniema, Tshopo, Kasaï, Sud-Ubangi, Maï-Ndombe, Kwango, Kinshasa, Kongo Central) restent sous surveillance. Les dix provinces restantes du pays n'ont pas rapporté de foyer épidémique majeur durant cette période. L'Est du pays concentre la majorité absolue des cas cumulés en raison de la fragilité des infrastructures d'accès à l'eau. Le trafic fluvial le long du fleuve Congo agit comme un vecteur clé de propagation du choléra vers les provinces de l'Ouest

fields.title: Flash Updates #57 Nouvel afflux de réfugiés soudanais au Tchad (21 Septembre 2026)
fields.body:
La situation sécuritaire le long des frontières tchadiennes demeure préoccupante, bien qu’elle reste globalement stable à l’intérieur du pays. Les provinces frontalières du Sila, de l’Ouaddaï, du Wadi-Fira et de l’Ennedi-Est continuent de subir les répercussions du conflit au Soudan voisin. Depuis la fin du mois d’août, outre les violences persistantes au Soudan qui continuent de contraindre des populations à chercher refuge au Tchad, le pays est également affecté par les retombées directes du conflit. Plusieurs frappes de drones ont ainsi été signalées dans les provinces du Wadi-Fira et de l’Ennedi-Est. Le 11 septembre, dans une localité près de Koulbous dans la province du Wadi-Fira, un ressortissant tchadien aurait été tué par des éléments des Forces de soutien rapide (FSR). Des cas d’enlèvements auraient également été rapportés dans cette zone frontalière.

Par ailleurs, la dégradation des conditions climatiques et les effets de la sécheresse, qualifiée par le Programme alimentaire mondial (PAM) comme l’une des plus sévères enregistrées dans la région depuis 1984, continuent d’affecter les moyens de subsistance, de compromettre les récoltes et d’alimenter de nouveaux mouvements de population vers l’est du Tchad. Face à cette situation, le Gouvernement tchadien a conduit ces dernières semaines une mission d’évaluation dans les provinces orientales afin d’apprécier l’ampleur du déficit pluviométrique et d’identifier des mesures d’atténuation adaptées. Parmi les réponses envisagées figurent notamment l’exonération des droits de douane sur certains produits alimentaires de première nécessité ainsi que la distribution ciblée de céréales aux ménages les plus affectés.

La problématique de la sécheresse a également été abordée lors des échanges entre les autorités provinciales du Ouaddaï et le Directeur régional du HCR pour l’Afrique de l’Est, la Corne de l’Afrique et les Grands Lacs, ainsi que Coordonnateur régional pour la situation des réfugiés soudanais, à l’occasion de sa mission au Tchad du 17 au 21 septembre 2026.  
Les autorités tchadiennes ont exprimé leurs inquiétudes quant aux conséquences humanitaires et socio-économiques de cette crise climatique, qui vient s’ajouter aux pressions engendrées par l’afflux continu de réfugiés soudanais.

À l’intérieur du pays, des incidents de criminalité et de petite délinquance, notamment des vols à main armée, des agressions et des explosions d’engins explosifs, continuent d’être signalés dans certaines zones accueillant des réfugiés. En parallèle, les fortes pluies saisonnières et la montée des eaux des ouadis entravent l’accès à plusieurs localités de l’est du Tchad, compliquant la mise en œuvre des opérations humanitaires.

Deux sessions de formation Safe and Secure Approaches in Field Environments (SSAFE) ont été organisées au profit de 61 participants et deux sessions supplémentaires, menées en collaboration avec le PAM, sont prévues en octobre.

fields.title: Ebola Bundibugyo Virus Disease Outbreak Democratic Republic of the Congo | Uganda Weekly External Situation Report 19, Data as of 20 September 2026
fields.body:
**Event description**  
The Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD) outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has expanded further, with Dungu Health Zone in Haut-Uélé Province, bordering South Sudan, being the latest affected, bringing the total number of health zones affected to 63 since the start of the outbreak. This latest geographic expansion heightens concern about further spread towards international borders, while transmission within the country remains increasingly heterogeneous across affected provinces and health zones. Since External Situation Report #18, a further 475 confirmed cases and 222 confirmed deaths have been reported, bringing the cumulative total to 7733 confirmed cases, including 3732 deaths \[crude case fatality ratio (CFR 48.3%)\], as of 20 September 2026. Ituri remains the principal focus, although its relative contribution continues to decline, accounting for 76.9% of cumulative confirmed cases, while substantial transmission continues in Nord-Kivu and persists in Haut-Uélé.

At the national level, daily incidence remains high and fluctuating, with the seven-day moving average rebounding in early September before declining in the most recent days. This national pattern masks divergent provincial trajectories. Ituri continues a gradual decline from its late-July peak but remains at a high level, while Nord-Kivu experienced a marked increase, reaching its highest incidence in mid-September, followed by an apparent decline in recent days. Transmission in Haut-Uélé remains sustained but below its August peak, while Tshopo shows renewed activity from a low baseline. Bas-Uélé continues to report sporadic transmission, with no recent transmission evident in Sud-Kivu. Overall, the epidemic remains geographically heterogeneous, with recent declines in the principal transmission areas occurring alongside persistent low-level transmission and continued geographic expansion to new areas.

fields.title: Crisis Analysis Team - Ebola incident analysis August 2026
fields.body:
**Summary :**

From 1 to 31 August 2026, the Crisis Analysis Team (CAT) documented 73 incidents related to the Ebola response, compared with 97 in July, a decrease of 25% and a rate of 16.5 incidents per week against 23 the previous month.

The human toll rose slightly, from 31 to 33 victims (2 deaths, 29 injured, 2 abducted), equivalent to 45 victims per 100 incidents compared with 32 in July. Two coercion incidents account for most of this: six civilians injured by the FARDC in Bunia and six people beaten at an M23 checkpoint in Kirumba, together 12 of the month’s 29 injured.

Sources of friction persist despite the fall in the volume of incidents. Violence against prevention and awareness-raising fell from 20 to 18 incidents, but its share rose from 21% to 25%; incidents related to safe and dignified burials (SDB) fell from 21 to 17. Financial grievances held steady, at 14 incidents against 15, but shifted from Bunia and Rwampara to Mongbwalu, Lita, Tchomia, Nizi, Kisangani and Avakubi.

Health facilities remain a direct target and are now being attacked repeatedly: the Mongbwalu ETC was set on fire on 18 August, the Bethesda dispensary in Katwa on the 27th, and the Bora Maisha hospital centre in Butembo twice in eleven days. These attacks follow narratives linking transfers, health workers or collaboration with the response to deaths that have occurred.

Risk is both concentrating and shifting. Beni is the only critical zone, with a score of 29, compared with four critical zones in July; Butembo (from 31 to 16), Bunia (from 28 to 11) and Katwa (from 1 to 12) are at the high level. Nyankunde, Nia-Nia and Rwampara declined markedly, Alimbongo recorded no further incidents and Mongbwalu returned to the moderate level. At the same time, the share of Ituri and North Kivu fell from 96% to 86%, while Tshopo rose from 3 to 8 incidents, with the emergence of Kabondo, and Haut-Uélé from 1 to 2.

Eight incidents are directly attributed to armed actors: four to the M23 on the Lubero axes, the others to CODECO, the Sambaza FDBC militia, the FARDC and a soldier in Kisangani. They are a matter for access negotiation, not awareness-raising.

Three risk systems therefore call for distinct responses: community friction around SDBs, prevention and health facilities; internal protest linked to payments; and armed control of movement and health measures. Physical protection of facilities is becoming a priority in Butembo and Katwa. For the coming month, there are five points of vigilance: the resumption of care in Butembo and Katwa, arrears owed to providers and training participants, developments in Mongbwalu, the safety of outreach teams in Beni and Bafwasende, and restrictions on the Lubero axes.

fields.title: Crisis Analysis Team - Analyse d'incidents Ebola août 2026
fields.body:
**Résumé**

Du 1er au 31 août 2026, le Crisis Analysis Team (CAT) a documenté 73 incidents liés à la riposte Ebola, contre 97 en juillet, soit une baisse de 25 % et un rythme de 16,5 incidents par semaine contre 23 le mois précédent.  
 Le bilan humain progresse légèrement, passant de 31 à 33 victimes (2 décès, 29 blessés, 2 enlevés), soit 45 victimes pour 100 incidents contre 32 en juillet. Deux incidents de coercition en expliquent l’essentiel : six civils blessés par les FARDC à Bunia et six personnes frappées à une barrière du M23 à Kirumba, soit 12 des 29 blessés du mois.  
 Les motifs de friction persistent malgré la baisse du volume d’incidents. Les violences contre la prévention et la sensibilisation passent de 20 à 18 incidents, mais leur part monte de 21 % à 25 % ; les incidents liés aux enterrements dignes et sécurisés (EDS) passent de 21 à 17. Les griefs financiers se maintiennent, 14 incidents contre 15, mais se déplacent de Bunia et Rwampara vers Mongbwalu, Lita, Tchomia, Nizi, Kisangani et Avakubi.  
 Les structures de soins restent une cible directe, désormais attaquée de façon répétée : incendie du CTE de Mongbwalu le 18 août, du dispensaire Bethesda à Katwa le 27, et à deux reprises en onze jours du centre hospitalier Bora Maisha à Butembo. Ces attaques suivent des récits liant les transferts, les soignants ou la collaboration avec la riposte aux décès survenus.  
 Le risque se concentre et se déplace. Beni est la seule zone critique, avec un score de 29, contre quatre zones critiques en juillet ; Butembo (de 31 à 16), Bunia (de 28 à 11) et Katwa (de 1 à 12) sont au niveau élevé. Nyankunde, Nia-Nia et Rwampara reculent nettement, Alimbongo n’enregistre plus d’incident et Mongbwalu revient au niveau modéré. Dans le même temps, la part de l’Ituri et du Nord-Kivu passe de 96 % à 86 % ; tandis que la Tshopo passe de 3 à 8 incidents, avec l’apparition de Kabondo, et le Haut-Uélé de 1 à 2.  
 Huit incidents sont directement attribués à des acteurs armés : quatre au M23 sur les axes du Lubero, les autres à la CODECO, aux miliciens Sambaza FDBC, aux FARDC et à un militaire à Kisangani. Ils relèvent de la négociation d’accès, non de la sensibilisation.  
 Trois systèmes de risque appellent donc des réponses distinctes : la friction communautaire autour des EDS, de la prévention et des structures ; la contestation interne liée aux paiements ; le contrôle armé des déplacements et des mesures sanitaires. La protection physique des structures devient prioritaire à Butembo et Katwa. Pour le mois à venir, cinq points de vigilance : la reprise des soins à Butembo et Katwa, les arriérés dus aux prestataires et aux participants aux formations, l’évolution de Mongbwalu, la sécurité des équipes de proximité à Beni et Bafwasende, et les restrictions sur les axes du Lubero.

fields.title: MSF expands response to Ebola disease with new treatment centres as outbreak spreads across provinces
fields.body:
In northeastern [Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC)](https://www.msf.org/democratic-republic-congo-drc), Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) is expanding our response to the [Ebola disease outbreak](https://www.msf.org/drc-ebola-outbreaks), as it spreads from the remote town of Nia Nia, in Ituri province, to Kisangani, the busy capital of neighbouring Tshopo province.  
  
In Kisangani, MSF has been running the Ebola treatment centre (ETC) at Hôpital du Cinquantenaire, in collaboration with the Ministry of Health, since the end of June. In the first week of September, patients were transferred to a new 22-bed ETC, built and run by MSF, increasing treatment capacity in Kisangani.  
  
In Nia Nia, MSF teams started working alongside the Ministry of Health at the ETC in the local hospital in early August. This week, MSF opened a new 50-bed ETC next to the hospital, further expanding access to [Ebola](https://www.msf.org/ebola) care in the area.

The two locations are closely connected. Nia Nia is situated in an area with significant movement of people and goods between Ituri, Tshopo and Haut-Uele provinces. Since the first cases were reported there, people infected in or linked to Nia Nia have travelled to other areas, including Kisangani. Thirteen of the 14 positive cases recorded in Kisangani as of 1 September had an epidemiological link to Nia Nia.

## Responding where the outbreak is spreading

Nia Nia has become a major focus of the [outbreak](https://www.msf.org/epidemics-and-pandemics) in southern Ituri. The town recorded its first cases at the end of June, but the response has faced significant challenges, including limited access to healthcare, gaps in infection prevention and control, and fear and misinformation within the community.  
  
MSF teams began working in Nia Nia in early August. As of 1 September, the Nia Nia ETC had admitted 85 people with symptoms matching Ebola. Of these, 59 were confirmed Ebola cases, including 15 patients who died. MSF opened a 50-bed ETC next to the existing facility, with 16 beds for suspected cases and 34 for confirmed cases, this week. The new centre is designed to provide safer and more effective care, with the protocols and bio-safety measures needed to treat patients with Ebola.  
  
“In an Ebola treatment centre, what we can do is care for the individual patient, but epidemics are stopped in the community,” says Miriam Alia, MSF medical coordinator.

## When fear prevents people from seeking care

During the first weeks of the outbreak in Nia Nia, fewer patients were reaching the ETC than the number of confirmed deaths reported in the community. Many people remained at home rather than seeking care.  
  
There are now signs of change. More people are reaching the treatment centre alive, giving them the opportunity to receive early, supportive treatment.  
  
“Three weeks ago, we started receiving patients rather than only alerts about deaths in the community,” says Alia. “This is a major change because it means people are coming to the ETC earlier, when they develop symptoms.”  
  
From the beginning, the response in Nia Nia has faced strong resistance, with rumours and misinformation fuelling fear. These have included claims that Ebola did not exist or that medical staff were bringing the disease into communities. Health workers were threatened, and an earlier treatment centre in the region was attacked and destroyed on 30 June.  
  
“I didn’t believe that Ebola existed,” says Maurice, a recovered Ebola patient who was treated by MSF in Kisangani. “But when I was tested and found out that I had Ebola, that’s when I understood that it exists. But people still say that Ebola isn’t real. In my neighbourhood, in people’s homes, that’s what I used to hear.”

MSF teams are working with community leaders, health workers and other local organisations to understand concerns, address misinformation, and build acceptance of the response.  
  
“During Ebola outbreaks, we used to talk about two epidemics: the epidemic itself, and the epidemic of fear,” says Alia. “Now we have a third one: the epidemic of misinformation.”

## From Nia-Nia to Kisangani

The link between Nia Nia and Kisangani shows why containing the outbreak in hard-to-reach areas is critical.  
  
“In the past month, two other people were infected in Kisangani after coming into contact with a body that had arrived from Nia Nia,” says Amy Low, MSF project medical adviser in Kisangani.  
  
Also in the past week, three patients with an epidemiological link to Nia Nia died at the MSF-supported ETC in Kisangani.  
  
MSF is expanding our capacity in both locations. But treatment centres alone cannot stop Ebola. Surveillance, testing, contact tracing, infection prevention and control, early isolation, treatment and community engagement all need to work together to reduce transmission and ensure that communities, such as Nia Nia, are not left behind.

fields.title: République Centrafricaine : Matrice de suivi des déplacements - Tableau de bord des déplacements, Round 25 (30 juillet au 27 août 2026)
fields.body:
En réponse aux crises multiples en RCA, l’Organisation internationale pour les migrations (OIM) déploie depuis décembre 2013 la Matrice de suivi des déplacements (*Displacement Tracking Matrix* en anglais, DTM), un outil qui collecte des données sur les tendances de déplacements et les besoins humanitaires multisectoriels des populations affectées par les crises. À travers sa composante de suivi de la mobilité des populations, la DTM met à jour les tendances de déplacements en collectant des informations auprès d’informateurs clés (autorités locales, représentants des déplacés) au sein des localités et des sites d’accueil des déplacés internes et retournés. Ces informations sont partagées avec la communauté humanitaire afin d’informer les programmes de réponse stratégiques et opérationnels.

En août 2026, 381 483 PDI, 2 451 285 retournés anciens PDI et 614 144 retournés de l'étranger ont été recensés.
